claim: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is defined by common behavioral characteristics.
source: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is defined by common behavioral characteristics, raising the possibility of shared pathogenic mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that establishes the defining features of ASD.

claim: Six individuals from two distinct ASD subtypes (idiopathic and 16p11.2 deletion) have common reductions in neural precursor cell (NPC) neurite outgrowth.
source: Surprisingly, our iPSC studies find that six individuals from two distinct ASD subtypes, idiopathic and 16p11.2 deletion, have common reductions in neural precursor cell (NPC) neurite outgrowth and migration even though whole genome sequencing demonstrates no genetic overlap between the datasets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from iPSC studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Six individuals from two distinct ASD subtypes (idiopathic and 16p11.2 deletion) have common reductions in neural precursor cell (NPC) migration.
source: Surprisingly, our iPSC studies find that six individuals from two distinct ASD subtypes, idiopathic and 16p11.2 deletion, have common reductions in neural precursor cell (NPC) neurite outgrowth and migration even though whole genome sequencing demonstrates no genetic overlap between the datasets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from iPSC studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Whole genome sequencing demonstrates no genetic overlap between idiopathic and 16p11.2 deletion ASD datasets.
source: Surprisingly, our iPSC studies find that six individuals from two distinct ASD subtypes, idiopathic and 16p11.2 deletion, have common reductions in neural precursor cell (NPC) neurite outgrowth and migration even though whole genome sequencing demonstrates no genetic overlap between the datasets.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: An unbiased phospho-proteome screen identified hundreds of shared p-peptides between autism subtypes including the mTOR pathway.
source: To identify signaling differences that may contribute to these developmental defects, an unbiased phospho-(p)-proteome screen was performed. Surprisingly despite the genetic heterogeneity, hundreds of shared p-peptides were identified between autism subtypes including the mTOR pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by phospho-proteome analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: mTOR signaling alterations were confirmed in all NPCs across both ASD subtypes.
source: mTOR signaling alterations were confirmed in all NPCs across both ASD subtypes, and mTOR modulation rescued ASD phenotypes and reproduced autism NPC-associated phenotypes in control NPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data confirming mTOR signaling alterations.

claim: mTOR modulation rescued ASD phenotypes in NPCs.
source: mTOR signaling alterations were confirmed in all NPCs across both ASD subtypes, and mTOR modulation rescued ASD phenotypes and reproduced autism NPC-associated phenotypes in control NPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using small molecule modulators of mTOR.

claim: mTOR modulation reproduced autism NPC-associated phenotypes in control NPCs.
source: mTOR signaling alterations were confirmed in all NPCs across both ASD subtypes, and mTOR modulation rescued ASD phenotypes and reproduced autism NPC-associated phenotypes in control NPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using small molecule modulators of mTOR in control cells.

claim: Genetically distinct ASD subtypes have common defects in neurite outgrowth and migration which are driven by the shared pathogenic mechanism of mTOR signaling dysregulation.
source: Thus, our studies demonstrate that genetically distinct ASD subtypes have common defects in neurite outgrowth and migration which are driven by the shared pathogenic mechanism of mTOR signaling dysregulation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including neurite, migration, and mTOR modulation experiments.

claim: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are characterized by deficits in social interaction and communication and the presence of repetitive and restrictive interests and behaviors.
source: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are characterized by deficits in social interaction and communication and the presence of repetitive and restrictive interests and behaviors.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical definition of ASD, supported by citations.

claim: There is marked heterogeneity in both clinical presentation and etiological underpinnings among affected individuals with ASD.
source: Though these common impairments define ASD, there is marked heterogeneity in both clinical presentation and etiological underpinnings among affected individuals (Jones and Klin, 2009; Kim and Lord, 2013, Betancur, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: About 10–15% of autism cases are genetically defined and caused by single gene mutations or copy number variants (CNVs).
source: About 10–15% of autism cases are genetically defined and caused by single gene mutations or copy number variants (CNVs) while most of ASD etiology remains undefined or idiopathic.
evidence: This is a statement about the genetic architecture of ASD based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Most of ASD etiology remains undefined or idiopathic.
source: About 10–15% of autism cases are genetically defined and caused by single gene mutations or copy number variants (CNVs) while most of ASD etiology remains undefined or idiopathic.
evidence: This is a statement about the genetic architecture of ASD based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Several studies have uncovered the convergence of both rare and common variant ASD risk genes onto the developing mid-fetal cerebral cortex (8–24 weeks).
source: Several studies have uncovered the convergence of both rare and common variant ASD risk genes onto the developing mid-fetal cerebral cortex (8–24 weeks) (Willsey et al., 2013; Parikshak et al., 2013; Satterstrom et al., 2020; Grove et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: During the mid-fetal period (8–24 weeks), neural precursor cells (NPCs) undergo proliferation, migration, and differentiation to form neurons and establish normal brain cytoarchitecture.
source: During this period, neural precursor cells (NPCs) undergo proliferation, migration, and differentiation to form neurons and establish normal brain cytoarchitecture (Liszewska and Jaworski, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: All three I-ASD NPCs had a significantly lower percentage of neurites than their respective Sibs (50–60% reduction, p<0.001 for all families).
source: Yet, surprisingly, we found that all three I-ASD NPCs had a significantly lower percentage of neurites than their respective Sibs (Figure 1B, 50–60% reduction, p<0.001 for all families).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All three I-ASD patients exhibited decreased migration (~30–50%) compared to their Sib (p<0.001).
source: Remarkably, we found that all three I-ASD patients exhibited decreased migration (~30–50%) compared to their Sib (p<0.001; Figure 1D) as well as unrelated Sibs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 16pDel NPCs have a lower percentage of neurites (7.4%) than both the Sib (11.3%, p<0.001) and NIH controls (12.7%, p<0.001).
source: Fascinatingly, 16pDel NPCs have a lower percentage of neurites (7.4%) than both the Sib (11.3%, p<0.001) and NIH controls (12.7%, p<0.001) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 16pDel NPCs have a higher percent of neurites than I-ASD (7.4% vs 5.1%, p<0.01).
source: Interestingly, 16pDel NPCs do have a higher percent of neurites than I-ASD (7.4% vs 5.1%, p<0.01) indicating potential subgroup differences.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the two ASD subtypes.

claim: All three 16pDel NPCs have impaired migration when compared to Sib and NIH NPCs.
source: Once again, like I-ASD NPCs, all three 16pDel NPCs have impaired migration when compared to Sib and NIH NPCs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Sib NPCs from all families had significant increases (45–75%, p<0.001) in neurites under PACAP, NGF, and 5-HT stimulation.
source: Under PACAP, NGF, and 5-HT stimulation, Sib NPCs from all families had significant increases (45–75%, p<0.001) in neurites (Figure 2A and B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and supplement.

claim: All three I-ASD NPCs failed to respond to PACAP, NGF, and 5-HT.
source: In contrast, all three I-ASD NPCs failed to respond to the three EFs (Figure 2A and B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and supplement.

claim: All three 16pDel NPCs respond to EFs with increases in neurite outgrowth.
source: Surprisingly, unlike I-ASD NPCs, all three 16pDel NPCs respond to EFs with increases in neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing 16pDel and I-ASD responses to extracellular factors.

claim: PACAP increased cell migration in all Sib NPCs but failed to stimulate migration in all I-ASD NPCs.
source: Like our neurite results, increased cell migration in Sibs was observed but there was no effect of PACAP on migration in any of the three I-ASD NPCs (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All three 16pDel NPCs and NIH NPCs respond to PACAP with increased migration.
source: Likewise, all three 16pDel NPCs and NIH NPCs respond to PACAP with increased migration (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: I-ASD proteome had nine changes while 16pDel had 48 changes compared to Sib (with log p>5 threshold).
source: With these parameters, I-ASD proteome had nine changes while 16pDel had 48 changes compared to Sib.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic analysis data.

claim: There were only three proteins (TAPT-1, GGA-1, S100A11) in common between I-ASD and 16pDel proteomes.
source: There were only three proteins (TAPT-1, GGA-1, S100A11) in common between I-ASD and 16pDel proteomes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: I-ASD NPCs had 105 differentially phosphorylated proteins compared to Sib with 149 unique phosphorylation sites.
source: In striking contrast, many more changes were observed in the p-proteome analysis: I-ASD NPCs had 105 differentially phosphorylated proteins compared to Sib with 149 unique phosphorylation sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by phospho-proteomic analysis data.

claim: 16pDel NPCs had 419 differentially phosphorylated proteins with 916 unique phosphorylation sites.
source: Further, 16pDel NPCs had 419 differentially phosphorylated proteins with 916 unique phosphorylation sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by phospho-proteomic analysis data.

claim: There is considerable overlap between I-ASD and 16pDel p-proteome results with 67 p-proteins (67/105) and 107 phosphorylation sites (107/149) shared.
source: Surprisingly, given the absence of genetic overlap between the cohorts, there is considerable overlap between I-ASD and 16pDel p-proteome results with 67 p-proteins (67/105) and 107 phosphorylation sites (107/149) shared between I-ASD and 16pDel (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phospho-proteomic analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The top three enriched modules in I-ASD p-proteome are tight junction signaling, mTOR signaling, and synaptogenesis signaling.
source: IPA of I-ASD p-proteome determined the top three enriched modules are tight junction signaling, mTOR signaling, and synaptogenesis signaling (Figure 3C, ).
evidence: This claim is supported by IPA analysis of phospho-proteomic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For the 16pDel p-proteome, the top three pathways are EIF2 signaling, regulation of EIF4 and p70S6K signaling, and mTOR signaling.
source: For the 16pDel p-proteome, the top three pathways are EIF2 signaling, regulation of EIF4 and p70S6K signaling, and mTOR signaling (Figure 3D, ).
evidence: This claim is supported by IPA analysis of phospho-proteomic data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The three most overlapping pathways between I-ASD and 16pDel are mTOR signaling, telomerase signaling, and HIPPO signaling.
source: Comparison analysis indicated the three most overlapping pathways between I-ASD and 16pDel as mTOR signaling, telomerase signaling, and HIPPO signaling (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative IPA analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: p-S6 dysregulation was found in all six ASD NPCs from both cohorts.
source: Remarkably, p-S6 dysregulation was found in all six ASD NPCs from both cohorts (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4.

claim: I-ASD-1 had a 75% reduction in p-S6 compared to Sib-1.
source: In the I-ASD cohort, Family-1 (I-ASD-1) had a 75% reduction in p-S6 compared to Sib-1 (Figure 4A and B)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: I-ASD-3 had a 45% reduction in p-S6 compared to Sib-3 (p < 0.001).
source: while I-ASD-3 from Family-3 had a 45% reduction in p-S6 compared to Sib-3 (Figure 4C and D, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: I-ASD-2 had elevated levels of p-S6 (260% increase, p < 0.001) when compared to Sib-2.
source: Surprisingly, in contrast, I-ASD-2 from Family-2 had elevated levels of p-S6 (Figure 4E and F, 260% increase, p < 0.001) when compared to Sib-2.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: All three 16pDel patient NPCs had higher p-S6 levels compared to both Sib and NIH NPCs (M1: ~170%, p < 0.0001, M2: ~130%, p < 0.001, F: ~80%, p < 0.01 increase).
source: In the 16pDel group, all three 16pDel patient NPCs had higher p-S6 levels compared to both Sib and NIH NPCs (M1: ~170%, p < 0.0001, M2: ~130%, p < 0.001, F: ~80%, p < 0.01 increase, Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: SC-79 (2 µg/mL) increased p-S6 levels in I-ASD-1 NPCs to that of Sib.
source: Focusing first on Family-1, addition of the SC-79 activator (2 µg/mL) to I-ASD-1 NPCs increased p-S6 levels to that of Sib (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: SC-79 increased the percentage of neurites and migration in I-ASD-1 NPCs without changing these parameters in Sib.
source: Indeed, SC-79 increased the percentage of neurites (Figure 5C) and migration in I-ASD NPCs (Figure 5D) without changing these parameters in Sib.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: MK-2206 (30 nM) reduced p-S6 levels in Sib-1 down to that of I-ASD-1.
source: MK-2206 (30 nM) reduced p-S6 levels in Sib down to that of I-ASD-1 (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: MK-2206 exposure reduced the percentage of neurites and migration of Sib-1 NPCs to that of I-ASD-1 NPCs.
source: MK-2206 exposure also reduced the percentage of neurites (Figure 5G) and migration (Figure 5H) of Sib-1 NPCs to that of I-ASD-1 NPCs thereby reproducing both the ASD neurite and migration defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: SC-79 increased p-S6 levels to that of Sib-3 in I-ASD-3.
source: Like in I-ASD-1, SC-79 increased p-S6 levels to that of Sib-3 in I-ASD-3 (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: SC-79 led to an increase in neurite outgrowth in I-ASD-3 that paralleled Sib-3 NPCs.
source: Likewise, SC-79 also led to an increase in neurite outgrowth in I-ASD-3 that paralleled Sib-3 NPCs (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Inhibiting p-S6 with MK-2206 in Sib-3 led to a reduction in neurite outgrowth that mimics the phenotype seen in I-ASD-3 NPCs.
source: Likewise, inhibiting p-S6 with MK-2206 in Sib-3 (Figure 5K) led to a reduction in neurite outgrowth that mimics the phenotype seen in I-ASD-3 NPCs (Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K and L.

claim: Addition of MK-2206 inhibitor reduced the levels of p-S6 in I-ASD-2 to that of Sib without changing total S6 levels.
source: Starting with I-ASD-2, addition of MK-2206 inhibitor reduced the levels of p-S6 to that of Sib without changing total S6 levels (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: MK-2206 increased both neurite outgrowth and migration in I-ASD-2 paralleling levels seen in Sib, thereby rescuing the phenotypes.
source: This increased both neurite outgrowth and migration paralleling levels seen in Sib, thereby rescuing the phenotypes (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: SC-79 increased p-S6 levels in Sib-2 NPCs to that of I-ASD-2.
source: SC-79 increased p-S6 levels in Sib-2 NPCs to that of I-ASD-2 (Figure 6E and F)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: SC-79 led to neurite and migration impairments in Sib-2 that mimic those seen in I-ASD-2.
source: which remarkably led to neurite and migration impairments that mimic those seen in I-ASD-2 (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Reducing p-S6 levels with inhibitor MK-2206 rescued the 16pDel phenotypes as shown by increased neurite outgrowth.
source: Reducing p-S6 levels with inhibitor MK-2206 (Figure 6I) rescued the 16pDel phenotypes as shown by increased neurite outgrowth (Figure 6J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: Increasing p-S6 with activator SC-79 in NIH NPCs reproduced the neurite defects noted in the 16pDel NPCs.
source: Conversely, increasing p-S6 with activator SC-79 (Figure 6K) in NIH NPCs reproduced the neurite defects noted in the 16pDel NPCs (Figure 6L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6K and L.

claim: Both over- and under-activation of mTOR signaling leads to common reduction in neurites and migration.
source: In summary, we find that both over- and under-activation of mTOR signaling leads to common reduction in neurites and migration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data from both high and low mTOR groups.

claim: Treatment of I-ASD-1 NPCs with subthreshold dose of SC-79 (0.1 µg/mL) results in NPCs responding to EFs.
source: However, when combined with PACAP, NGF, and 5-HT, the I-ASD-1 NPCs now responded to all three EFs (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Treatment of Sib-1 NPCs with subthreshold MK-2206 (1 nM) abolishes NPC response to EFs.
source: Addition of 'subthreshold' MK-2206 (1 nM) to Sib-1 NPCs abolished their typical EF responses (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Using a 'subthreshold' dose of inhibitor (1 nM MK-2206), I-ASD-2 NPCs were able to respond to EFs.
source: Finally, we also examined high mTOR Family-2: using a 'subthreshold' dose of inhibitor (1 nM MK-2206), I-ASD-2 NPCs were now able to respond to EFs (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: No I-ASD individual had rare non-synonymous protein-coding variants in the 28 genes deleted in 16p11.2.
source: Moreover, no I-ASD individual had rare non-synonymous protein-coding variants in the 28 genes deleted in 16p11.2.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing analysis.

claim: There are no rare protein-coding non-synonymous genetic variants shared between all three I-ASD individuals.
source: Finally, there are no rare protein-coding non-synonymous genetic variants shared between all three I-ASD individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing analysis.

claim: The 16p11.2 CNV deletes 28 genes.
source: The CNV deletes 28 genes, increases autism risk by ~20-fold, and is one of the most common ASD-associated mutations (Weiss et al., 2008; Niarchou et al., 2019; Qureshi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The 16p11.2 CNV increases autism risk by ~20-fold.
source: The CNV deletes 28 genes, increases autism risk by ~20-fold, and is one of the most common ASD-associated mutations (Weiss et al., 2008; Niarchou et al., 2019; Qureshi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The 16p11.2 CNV is one of the most common ASD-associated mutations.
source: The CNV deletes 28 genes, increases autism risk by ~20-fold, and is one of the most common ASD-associated mutations (Weiss et al., 2008; Niarchou et al., 2019; Qureshi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Neurite outgrowth is a critical cytoskeleton-dependent process necessary for normal neural connectivity in the brain.
source: Within differentiation, neurite outgrowth is a critical cytoskeleton-dependent process necessary for normal neural connectivity in the brain.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Multiple studies of NDDs have reported impairment in neurite outgrowth.
source: Elaboration of neurites is an important mechanism to assess for proper development in neuronal cells and multiple studies of NDDs have reported impairment in neurite outgrowth (Gleeson and Walsh, 2000; Uppal and Hof, 2013; Wegiel et al., 2010; Kathuria et al., 2018; Doers et al., 2014; Marchetto et al., 2010; Krey et al., 2013; Deshpande et al., 2017; Prem et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Alterations in migration have been reported in multiple NDDs.
source: Moreover, alterations in migration have been reported in multiple NDDs as well (Wegiel et al., 2010; Wiegreffe et al., 2015; Hori and Hoshino, 2017; Prem et al., 2020; Brennand et al., 2011b; Brennand and Gage, 2011a, Brennand et al., 2011c, Brennand et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: IPA of total proteome data did not find any mTOR enrichment in either I-ASD or 16pDel NPCs.
source: In striking contrast, IPA of total proteome data even with threshold log p > 3 did not find any mTOR enrichment in either I-ASD or 16pDel NPCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by IPA analysis of total proteome data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: I-ASD WGS did not show any mTOR pathway enrichment with canonical pathway analyses or with network analysis.
source: Much like the total proteome results, I-ASD WGS did not show any mTOR pathway enrichment with canonical pathway analyses or with network analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by IPA analysis of WGS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Total S6 and AKT protein levels were not different between any of the NPCs.
source: Importantly, total S6 and AKT protein levels were not different between any of the NPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing no changes in total protein levels.

claim: There were no statistical differences in p-S6 levels between Sib and NIH NPCs (p = 0.99).
source: There were no statistical differences in p-S6 levels between Sib and NIH NPCs (p = 0.99).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of western blot data.

claim: All 16pDel NPCs displayed higher p-AKT levels compared to NIH but not Sib NPCs.
source: All 16pDel NPCs also displayed higher p-AKT levels compared to NIH but not Sib NPCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Tight regulation of mTOR pathway is essential for normal neural development.
source: Manipulation of mTOR could rescue or reproduce ASD phenotypes in both low and high mTOR NPCs, indicating that tight regulation of mTOR pathway is essential for normal neural development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that both increases and decreases in mTOR lead to phenotypes.

claim: Monogenic syndromic disorders which can exhibit ASD such as tuberous sclerosis (TSC), PTEN-associated ASD, and neurofibromatosis-1 have mutations that directly affect mTOR pathway components.
source: Consistent with the idea that mTOR signaling dysfunction could be a common mechanism for autism, monogenic syndromic disorders, which can exhibit ASD such as tuberous sclerosis (TSC), PTEN-associated ASD, and neurofibromatosis-1, have mutations that directly affect mTOR pathway components (Enriquez-Barreto and Morales, 2016; Yeung et al., 2017; Huber et al., 2015; Dasgupta et al., 2005; Winden et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2010; Rangasamy et al., 2016; Costales and Kolevzon, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some studies of syndromic diseases where the driving mutation is not in the mTOR pathway, such as Fragile-X, Angelman, Rett syndrome, and Phelan-McDermid syndrome (22q13 deletion), also show mTOR alterations in human postmortem samples, embryonic stem cell models, and hiPSC-based models.
source: Furthermore, some studies of syndromic diseases where the driving mutation is not in the mTOR pathway, such as Fragile-X, Angelman, Rett syndrome, and Phelan-McDermid syndrome (22q13 deletion), also show mTOR alterations in human postmortem samples, embryonic stem cell models, and hiPSC-based models (Winden et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In 16pDel, because the MAPK3 gene is deleted, both rodent and human studies have uncovered alterations in ERK1 signaling.
source: In 16pDel, because the MAPK3 gene is deleted, both rodent and human studies have uncovered alterations in ERK1 signaling (Pucilowska et al., 2018; Pucilowska et al., 2015; Deshpande et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Altered mTOR has not been reported previously in 16pDel.
source: Importantly for 16pDel, altered mTOR has not been reported previously.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding in the context of existing literature.

claim: Recent studies in peripheral white blood cells identified mTOR signaling proteins and p-proteins as being predictors of not only ASD diagnosis but also disease severity.
source: However, recent studies in peripheral white blood cells identified mTOR signaling proteins and p-proteins as being predictors of not only ASD diagnosis but also disease severity (Onore et al., 2017; Rosina et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Human iPSC-derived NPCs are similar transcriptionally and functionally to cortical NPCs.
source: Given that human iPSC-derived NPCs are similar transcriptionally and functionally to cortical NPCs, our studies provide experimental evidence of NPC developmental dysregulation in ASD (Hofrichter et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: About a third of the overlapping p-proteins between I-ASD and 16pDel are common with 102 high confidence ASD risk genes or relevant gene families.
source: Further, about a third of these p-proteins are common with 102 high confidence ASD risk genes or relevant gene families (Satterstrom et al., 2020), suggesting that we are identifying similar pathways as described by others.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published ASD risk genes and citation.

claim: The I-ASD p-proteome has 38 differently phosphorylated proteins that are not shared with the 16pDel.
source: Specifically, the I-ASD p-proteome has 38 differently phosphorylated proteins that are not shared with the 16pDel
evidence: This claim is supported by phospho-proteomic analysis data.

claim: The 16pDel p-proteome has 351 differently phosphorylated proteins not shared with the I-ASD NPCs.
source: and the 16pDel p-proteome has 351 differently phosphorylated proteins not shared with the I-ASD NPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by phospho-proteomic analysis data.

claim: I-ASD NPCs seem to have dysregulation in tight junction signaling as well as in proteins such as spectrin and ankyrin which are essential to appropriate stabilization of membrane proteins.
source: Analysis of these 'differently' expressed p-proteins show that I-ASD NPCs seem to have dysregulation in tight junction signaling as well as in proteins such as spectrin and ankyrin which are essential to appropriate stabilization of membrane proteins (such as signaling receptors) to the underlying cytoskeleton.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of phospho-proteomic data.

claim: About 30% of children with ASD have elevations in blood 5-HT.
source: Indeed, meta-analyses have found that about 30% of children with ASD have elevations in blood 5-HT.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from meta-analyses in the field.

claim: The I-ASD cohort was selected from the New Jersey Language and Autism Genetics Study.
source: The I-ASD cohort was selected from the previously reported New Jersey Language and Autism Genetics Study.
evidence: This is a description of the study cohort source.

claim: iPSCs were generated from three male probands with ASD and their sex-matched unaffected siblings (Sib) served as controls.
source: From three separate families, iPSCs were generated from three male probands with ASD and their sex-matched unaffected siblings (Sib) served as controls (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the study design and sample generation.

claim: The 16p11.2 deletion cohort consists of three individuals, two males (16pDel M-1, 16pDel M-2) and one female (16pDel F).
source: This cohort consists of three individuals, two males (16pDel M-1, 16pDel M-2) and one female (16pDel F).
evidence: This is a description of the study cohort composition.

claim: Three iPSC lines from the NIH Regenerative Medicine Program were selected as sex-matched controls for the 16p11.2 deletion cohort.
source: For sex-matched controls, we selected three iPSC lines from the NIH Regenerative Medicine Program (NIH).
evidence: This is a description of the control selection for the study.

claim: Two to five clones per individual (except for NIH) and two to five independent neural inductions were analyzed to ensure extensive rigor and reproducibility.
source: We analyzed these 12 individuals (six I-ASD-Sib and six 16pDel-NIH) extensively for developmental phenotypes utilizing two to five clones per individual (except for NIH) and two to five independent neural inductions to ensure extensive rigor and reproducibility (see Materials and methods and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for rigor and reproducibility.

claim: WGS demonstrated that no I-ASD individuals harbored the 16p11.2 deletion.
source: WGS was conducted on I-ASD dataset and demonstrated that no individuals harbored the 16p11.2 deletion (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: Differences in migration area were not related to the initial neurosphere size.
source: Moreover, differences in migration area were not related to the initial neurosphere size (see Materials and methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no difference in neurite extension between Sib NPCs (11.3%) and NIH NPCs (12.7%) (p=0.1).
source: There was no difference in neurite extension between Sib NPCs (11.3%) and NIH NPCs (12.7%) (p=0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were no differences in migration between 16pDel and I-ASD or Sib NPCs and NIH NPCs.
source: There were no differences in migration between 16pDel and I-ASD or Sib NPCs and NIH NPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The lack of response to EFs in I-ASD was not due to differential sensitivities or inappropriate doses of EF, as dose-response analyses indicate Sibs respond to PACAP and NGF at multiple doses while ASD had no response at any physiological dose.
source: The lack of response was not due to differential sensitivities or inappropriate doses of EF, as dose-response analyses indicate Sibs respond to PACAP and NGF at multiple doses while ASD had no response at any physiological dose (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: NIH NPCs exhibit increases in neurite outgrowth by EF stimulation.
source: As expected, like Sib controls, NIH NPCs also exhibit increases in neurite outgrowth by EF stimulation (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, D, and supplement 3.

claim: For both I-ASD and 16pDel p-proteome, alterations in cytoskeleton, cell cycle, and developmental processes were identified by G-profiler analysis.
source: For both I-ASD and 16pDel p-proteome, alterations in cytoskeleton, cell cycle, and developmental processes were identified, correlating well with our defined cellular phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by G-profiler bioinformatics analysis of phospho-proteomic data.

claim: IPA expression network analysis of p-proteome reveals strongly altered p-S6 as a central node of convergence in both I-ASD and 16pDel networks along with other mTOR members.
source: Interestingly, IPA expression network analysis of p-proteome reveals strongly altered p-S6 as a central node of convergence in both I-ASD and 16pDel networks along with other mTOR members (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by IPA network analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Less significant changes were noted in p-AKT levels in all ASD NPCs.
source: Further, less significant changes were also noted in p-AKT levels in all ASD NPCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Western studies revealed two distinct groups of p-S6 dysregulation: one group with reduced p-S6 levels and another with elevated p-S6 levels.
source: While p-proteome analysis revealed p-S6 as a common dysregulated node among all ASD individuals (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2), our western studies revealed two distinct groups of p-S6 dysregulation. In one group, p-S6 levels were reduced relative to controls whereas in the other p-S6 levels were elevated, suggesting two distinct 'signaling subtypes' as described below.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing both increases and decreases in p-S6.

claim: SC-79 at 2 µg/mL had no effect on p-S6 levels in Sib-1.
source: Importantly, SC-79 at this dose had no effect on p-S6 levels in Sib, nor on the levels of total S6 in either Sib or I-ASD.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data.

claim: Sib-2 had no significant response to MK-2206 at the dose used for I-ASD-2.
source: Significantly, Sib-2 had no significant response to MK-2206 at this dose.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Addition of subthreshold SC-79 to Sib NPCs did not heighten EF response.
source: This rescue effect was specific to I-ASD-1 NPCs as addition of subthreshold SC-79 to Sib NPCs did not heighten EF response (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Subthreshold dose of SC-79 (0.1 µg/mL) did not stimulate neurite outgrowth in I-ASD-1 NPCs on its own.
source: For Family-1, agonist SC-79 (0.1 µg/mL) did not stimulate neurite outgrowth in I-ASD-1 NPCs (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.
